newsitem.title: UK: Gold is hit by a new wave of speculative sales.
newsitem.headline: Gold is hit by a new wave of speculative sales.

text.p: A new wave of selling depressed gold prices to levels not seen since October 1993 on Friday when speculators and professional dealers alike decided there was no profit in holding the yellow metal.
Gold had briefly shown some reluctance to fall below $364.00 per ounce at which it fixed in the afternoon.
But it dropped again soon afterwards to a low bid of $361.80. Gold had ended 1996 at almost $368.
"The tone is still bearish," one dealer said, while another referred to "gold's bearish internal combustion" as overwhelming any positive influence for the moment.

"It's not clear that there is enough fresh news in the market to replace the bearish psychology which prevailed before Christmas," said bullion market analyst Tony Warwick-Ching at research group CRU International.
"There is also some suggestion that demand has turned softer in (South East Asia) which is not helping," he said.

Part of the bearishness also came from the threat to the gold market from possible central bank selling, especially in Europe, which the banks were re-assessing their largely dormant and non-revenue earning gold reserves, several analyst said.
"Producer selling and central bank selling in response to a price rally will stop gold and silver going above their historic highs (in 1997)," one said.
Dealers noted that the market was still working at half speed after the Christmas and New Year holidays with many dealers not back at their desks yet and Japan closed for a week of national holdays.
But Warwick-Ching and some dealers dismissed as insignificant both these "seasonal factors" and the fact that industrial consumers of precious metals were out of the market over the holiday period.
Industrial precious metals users were expected to start returning but that was unlikely to change the outlook.
"Physical buying may slow the fall but the market will not turn round until the speculators begin to buy instead of sell," a dealer said.

Gold fixed at its all-time high of $850 per ounce in January 1980 when rising oil prices and inflation threatened the value of currencies across the Western world. Early last year gold reached a post-Gulf War peak when as the investment funds piled into the market and it topped $416.00. But the rally was short lived.
Platinum also lost about $1.50 on Friday after posting an afternoon fix of $366.00, a fresh low since November 2, 1993.
"There is not much on the upside and Japan being away doesn't help either," said one dealer.
Palladium held gains from fund buying on Nymex on Tuesday.
It was indicated at $120.00/$121.00 just 25 cents down overnight and against $116.50 at Tuesday's London close.
Silver managed a bounce off $4.66 to be indicated at $4.68/$4.70, down four cents.
"Historically the first few days of a New Year have set the tone for the first quarter, so it looks like weakness is set to continue for the moment," one senior bullion dealer said.
